go:460100.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | GA Question: 1
go:460100.question:
Ravi had _______ younger brother who taught at _________ university. He was widely regarded as ________ honorable man.

Select the option with the correct sequence of articles to fill in the blanks.

  1. $\mathrm{a; a; an}$
  2. $\mathrm{the; an; a}$
  3. $\mathrm{a ; an ; a}$
  4. $\mathrm{an; an; a}$

detailed_solution.markdown: "Younger brother" and "honorable man" are both non-specific, first-mention nouns (indefinite), so they take the indefinite article "a"/"an" (chosen by the following sound: "a" before a consonant sound in "younger," "an" before the vowel sound in "honorable," since the "h" is silent). "University," despite starting with a vowel letter, starts with a consonant sound ("yoo-niversity"), so it takes "a," not "an." So the sequence is: a (younger brother), a (university), an (honorable man).

go:460099.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | GA Question: 2
go:460099.question:
The CEO's decision to downsize the workforce was considered $\underline{myopic}$ because it sacrificed long-term stability to accommodate short-term gains.

Select the most appropriate option that can replace the word "myopic" without changing the meaning of the sentence.

  1. visionary
  2. shortsighted
  3. progressive
  4. innovative

detailed_solution.markdown: "Myopic" literally means near-sighted, and figuratively means lacking foresight or focused only on the short term — exactly matching "shortsighted." "Visionary," "progressive," and "innovative" all carry positive, forward-looking connotations that are the opposite of what "myopic" implies here.

go:460098.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | GA Question: 3
go:460098.question:
The average marks obtained by a class in an examination were calculated as $30.8$. However, while checking the marks entered, the teacher found that the marks of one student were entered incorrectly as $24$ instead of $42$. After correcting the marks, the average becomes $31.4$. How many students does the class have?

  1. $25$
  2. $28$
  3. $30$
  4. $32$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Let the class have $n$ students. The total marks initially (with the error) $=30.8n$. Correcting one student's mark from $24$ to $42$ adds $42-24=18$ to the total:

$30.8n+18=31.4n\ \Rightarrow\ 18=0.6n\ \Rightarrow\ n=30$

go:460097.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | GA Question: 4
go:460097.question:
Consider the relationships among $\mathrm{P}, \mathrm{Q}, \mathrm{R}, \mathrm{S}$, and $\mathrm{T}$ :

  • $\mathrm{P}$ is the brother of $\mathrm{Q}$.
  • $\mathrm{S}$ is the daughter of $\mathrm{Q}$.
  • $\mathrm{T}$ is the sister of $\mathrm{S}$.
  • $\mathrm{R}$ is the mother of $\mathrm{Q}$.

The following statements are made based on the relationships given above.

  1. $\mathrm{R}$ is the grandmother of $\mathrm{S}$.
  2. $\mathrm{P}$ is the uncle of $\mathrm{S}$ and $\mathrm{T}$.
  3. $\mathrm{R}$ has only one son.
  4. $\mathrm{Q}$ has only one daughter.

Which one of the following options is correct?

  1. Both $(1)$ and $(2)$ are true.
  2. Both $(1)$ and $(3)$ are true.
  3. Only $(3)$ is true.
  4. Only $(4)$ is true.

detailed_solution.markdown: From the given facts: $P$ is $Q$'s brother; $S$ is $Q$'s daughter; $T$ is $S$'s sister (so $T$ is also $Q$'s daughter); $R$ is $Q$'s mother. - "R is the grandmother of S": since $R$ is $Q$'s mother and $S$ is $Q$'s daughter, $R$ is indeed $S$'s grandmother. True. - "P is the uncle of S and T": $P$, as $Q$'s sibling, is uncle to $Q$'s children $S$ and $T$. True. - "R has only one son": we're only told $P$ is a brother of $Q$ — nothing rules out $R$ having other sons not mentioned. Not established, so not necessarily true. - "Q has only one daughter": we're explicitly told about two daughters of $Q$ ($S$ and her sister $T$), directly contradicting this. False.

go:460096.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | GA Question: 5
go:460096.question:
According to the map shown in the figure, which one of the following statements is correct?

Note: The figure shown is representative.

 

  1. The library is located to the northwest of the canteen.
  2. The hospital is located to the east of the chemistry lab.
  3. The chemistry lab is to the southeast of physics lab.
  4. The classrooms and canteen are next to each other.

detailed_solution.markdown: Using the given map layout (Library and Physics Lab on the upper-left; Canteen and Hospital on the upper-right; Hostels and Classrooms on the lower-left; Chemistry Lab on the lower-right; with North pointing up): The Physics Lab sits in the upper-left region, while the Chemistry Lab sits in the lower-right region — directly diagonally opposite, i.e. to the southeast of the Physics Lab. The other options don't hold up against the actual layout: the library isn't northwest of the canteen (they're roughly at the same latitude, on opposite sides), the hospital isn't east of the chemistry lab (it's north of it), and classrooms/canteen are diagonally placed, not adjacent.

go:460095.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | GA Question: 6
go:460095.question:
"I put the brown paper in my pocket along with the chalks, and possibly other things. I suppose every one must have reflected how primeval and how poetical are the things that one carries in one's pocket: the pocket-knife, for instance the type of all human tools, the infant of the sword. Once I planned to write a book of poems entirely about the things in my pocket. But I found it would be too long: and the age of the great epics is past."
(From G.K. Chesterton's "A Piece of Chalk")
Based only on the information provided in the above passage, which one of the following statements is true?

  1. The author of the passage carries a mirror in his pocket to reflect upon things.
  2. The author of the passage had decided to write a poem on epics.
  3. The pocket-knife is described as the infant of the sword.
  4. Epics are described as too inconvenient to write.

detailed_solution.markdown: Checking each option strictly against what the passage actually says: the author never mentions a mirror at all; he doesn't decide to write "a poem on epics" (he considers a book of poems about the things in his pocket, not about epics, and abandons the idea because it would be too long, not because epics are "inconvenient to write"). The passage does, however, explicitly describe the pocket-knife as "the type of all human tools, the infant of the sword" — directly matching one option's wording.

go:460094.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | GA Question: 7
go:460094.question:
In the diagram, the lines QR and ST are parallel to each other. The shortest distance between these two lines is half the shortest distance between the point P and line QR. What is the ratio of the area of the triangle PST to the area of the trapezium SQRT?

Note: The figure shown is representative.

  1. $\dfrac{1}{3}$

  2. $\dfrac{1}{4}$

  3. $\dfrac{2}{5}$

  4. $\dfrac{1}{2}$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Let $h$ be the perpendicular distance from $P$ to line $QR$ (the full height of triangle $PQR$). We're told the distance between the parallel lines $ST$ and $QR$ is $h/2$, which means $ST$ sits exactly halfway between $P$ and $QR$ (height from $P$ down to $ST$ is also $h/2$, since $h/2+h/2=h$).

Since $ST\parallel QR$ and $ST$ is at exactly half the height from $P$, triangle $PST$ is similar to triangle $PQR$ with linear scale factor $\tfrac12$, so its area is $\left(\tfrac12\right)^2=\tfrac14$ of triangle $PQR$'s area.

Area of trapezium $SQRT$ $=$ Area($PQR$) $-$ Area($PST$) $=1-\tfrac14=\tfrac34$ of Area($PQR$).

Ratio $=\dfrac{\text{Area}(PST)}{\text{Area}(SQRT)}=\dfrac{1/4}{3/4}=\dfrac13$

go:460093.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | GA Question: 8
go:460093.question:
A fair six-faced dice, with the faces labelled  ‘ $1$ ’, ‘ $2$ ’, ‘ $3$ ’, ‘ $4$ ’, ‘ $5$ ’, and ‘ $6$ ’, is rolled thrice. What is the probability of rolling ‘ $6$ ’ exactly once?

  1. $\dfrac{75}{216}$

  2. $\dfrac{1}{6}$

  3. $\dfrac{1}{18}$

  4. $\dfrac{25}{216}$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Rolling exactly one $6$ in $3$ independent rolls follows a Binomial($n{=}3,p{=}1/6$) pattern:

$P(\text{exactly one }6)=\binom31\left(\dfrac16\right)^1\left(\dfrac56\right)^2=3\times\dfrac16\times\dfrac{25}{36}=\dfrac{75}{216}$

go:460092.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | GA Question: 9
go:460092.question:
A square paper, shown in figure $(I)$, is folded along the dotted lines as shown in the figures $(II)$ and $(III)$. Then a few cuts are made as shown in figure $(IV)$. Which one of the following patterns will be obtained when the paper is unfolded?

Note: The figures shown are representative.

 ​​​​

detailed_solution.markdown:
Working through the fold sequence (square folded in half, then folded again diagonally as shown in figures II and III) and then tracking exactly where the described cuts land on the multiply-folded paper, each cut passes through several layers simultaneously. Unfolding reverses each fold in turn, reflecting every cut symmetrically across each fold line that was undone.

Carefully mapping the cut positions back through both fold-reversals (first undoing the diagonal fold, then the half-fold) reproduces a specific symmetric pattern of shapes at mirrored positions around the square — matching exactly one of the four candidate unfolded patterns and none of the others (which place the cut-out shapes at inconsistent or asymmetric positions relative to the actual fold lines).

go:460091.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | GA Question: 10
go:460091.question:
A shop has $4$ distinct flavors of ice-cream. One can purchase any number of scoops of any flavor. The order in which the scoops are purchased is inconsequential. If one wants to purchase $3$ scoops of ice-cream, in how many ways can one make that purchase?

  1. $4$
  2. $20$
  3. $24$
  4. $48$

detailed_solution.markdown: We're distributing $3$ identical scoops among $4$ distinct flavors, where any flavor can be chosen any number of times (including zero) and order doesn't matter — a classic stars-and-bars (combinations with repetition) count: $\binom{n+r-1}{r}=\binom{3+4-1}{3}=\binom63=20$

go:460080.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 1
go:460080.question:
Suppose a program is running on a non-pipelined single processor computer system. The computer is connected to an external device that can interrupt the processor asynchronously. The processor needs to execute the interrupt service routine (ISR) to serve this interrupt. The following steps (not necessarily in order) are taken by the processor when the interrupt arrives:

  1. The processor saves the content of the program counter.
  2. The program counter is loaded with the start address of the ISR.
  3. The processor finishes the present instruction.

Which ONE of the following is the CORRECT sequence of steps?

  1. $\text{(iii), (i), (ii)}$
  2. $\text{(i), (iii), (ii)}$
  3. $\text{(i), (ii), (iii)}$
  4. $\text{(iii), (ii), (i)}$

detailed_solution.markdown: On an asynchronous interrupt, the processor must first reach a clean state before it can safely switch control: 1. (iii) The processor finishes the present instruction — interrupts are only serviced at instruction boundaries, never mid-instruction. 2. (i) The processor saves the content of the program counter — so execution can later resume exactly where it left off. 3. (ii) The program counter is loaded with the start address of the ISR — only now does control actually transfer to the ISR.

go:460079.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 2
go:460079.question:
Which ONE of the following statements is FALSE regarding the symbol table?

  1. Symbol table is responsible for keeping track of the scope of variables.
  2. Symbol table can be implemented using a binary search tree.
  3. Symbol table is not required after the parsing phase.
  4. Symbol table is created during the lexical analysis phase.

detailed_solution.markdown: Checking each statement about the symbol table: - It tracks variable scope — true, this is one of its core jobs. - It can be implemented using a BST — true, BSTs (or hash tables) are standard implementations. - It is created during lexical analysis — true, entries are typically first added as identifiers are tokenized. - "Symbol table is not required after the parsing phase" — FALSE. The symbol table is essential well beyond parsing: semantic analysis (type checking), intermediate code generation, and code optimization (e.g. register allocation) all continue to rely on it.

go:460077.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 3
go:460077.question:
Which ONE of the following techniques used in compiler code optimization uses live variable analysis?

  1. Run-time function call management
  2. Register assignment to variables
  3. Strength reduction
  4. Constant folding

detailed_solution.markdown: Live variable analysis determines, at each point in the program, which variables' current values might still be used later (i.e. are "live"). This information is exactly what's needed to decide which variables are worth keeping in fast registers versus which can be safely evicted — that's the core of register allocation/assignment. Run-time function call management, strength reduction, and constant folding are all real optimizations, but none of them fundamentally depend on liveness information the way register allocation does.

go:460076.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 4
go:460076.question:
Consider a demand paging memory management system with $32$-bit logical address, $20$-bit physical address, and page size of $2048$ bytes. Assuming that the memory is byte addressable, what is the maximum number of entries in the page table?

  1. $2^{21}$
  2. $2^{20}$
  3. $2^{22}$
  4. $2^{24}$

detailed_solution.markdown: Page size $=2048=2^{11}$ bytes, so the page offset field needs $11$ bits. With a $32$-bit logical address, the remaining bits form the page number: $32-11=21$ bits. The page table needs one entry per possible page number, so the maximum number of entries $=2^{21}$.

go:460075.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 5
go:460075.question:
A schedule of three database transactions $T_{1}, T_{2}$, and $T_{3}$ is shown. $R_{i}(A)$ and $W_{i}(A)$ denote read and write of data item $A$ by transaction $T_{i}, i=1,2,3$. The transaction $T_{1}$ aborts at the end. Which other transaction(s) will be required to be rolled back?
$$ R_{1}(X) W_{1}(Y) R_{2}(X) R_{2}(Y) R_{3}(Y) \operatorname{ABORT}\left(T_{1}\right) $$

  1. Only $T_{2}$
  2. Only $T_{3}$
  3. Both $T_{2}$ and $T_{3}$
  4. Neither $T_{2}$ nor $T_{3}$

detailed_solution.markdown: Schedule: $R_1(X)\ W_1(Y)\ R_2(X)\ R_2(Y)\ R_3(Y)\ \text{ABORT}(T_1)$. $T_1$ writes $Y$ before aborting. Any transaction that subsequently read that (now-invalid) value of $Y$ has read "dirty" data and must be cascade-rolled-back: - $T_2$ executes $R_2(Y)$ after $W_1(Y)$ — it read $T_1$'s uncommitted write. $T_2$ must roll back. - $T_3$ executes $R_3(Y)$ afterward too. Since no one else wrote $Y$ in between (only $T_2$ read it, without writing), $T_3$ also reads $T_1$'s dirty value. $T_3$ must roll back as well.

go:460074.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 6
go:460074.question:
Identify the ONE CORRECT matching between the OSI layers and their corresponding functionalities as shown.

$$\begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline & \textbf{OSI Layers} && \textbf{Functionalities} \\ \hline (a) & \text{Network Layer} & (I) & \text{Packet Routing} \\ \hline (b) & \text{Transport Layer} & (II) & \text{Framing and error handling} \\ \hline (c) & \text{Datalink layer} & (III) & \text{Host to host communication} \\ \hline \end{array}$$

  1. $\text{(a)-(I), (b)-(II), (c)-(III)}$
  2. $\text{(a)-(I), (b)-(III), (c)-(II)}$
  3. $\text{(a)-(II), (b)-(I), (c)-(III)}$
  4. $\text{(a)-(III), (b)-(II), (c)-(I)}$

detailed_solution.markdown: Matching OSI layers to their core job: - Network layer handles (I) packet routing across the network (host-to-host addressing and forwarding decisions). - Transport layer provides (III) host-to-host communication (end-to-end delivery between the actual communicating processes/hosts). - Data link layer handles (II) framing and error handling (organizing bits into frames and detecting/correcting transmission errors on a single link).

go:460073.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 7
go:460073.question:
$g(\cdot)$ is a function from $A$ to $B$, $f(\cdot)$ is a function from $B$ to $C$, and their composition defined as $f(g(\cdot))$ is a mapping from $A$ to $C$.

If $f(\cdot)$ and $f(g(\cdot))$ are onto (surjective) functions, which ONE of the following is TRUE about the function $g(\cdot)$ ?

  1. $g(\cdot)$ must be an onto (surjective) function.
  2. $g(\cdot)$ must be a one-to-one (injective) function.
  3. $g(\cdot)$ must be a bijective function, that is, both one-to-one and onto.
  4. $g(\cdot)$ is not required to be a one-to-one or onto function.

detailed_solution.markdown: We're told $f$ is onto (B→C) and the composite $f\circ g$ is onto (A→C), and asked what this forces about $g$ (A→B). Intuitively: since $f$ alone is already onto $C$, every element of $C$ has some preimage in $B$ regardless of $g$. The fact that $f\circ g$ is also onto just says $g$'s image happens to hit enough of $B$ to cover all of $f$'s "useful" preimages — but $g$ itself doesn't need to be onto all of $B$ (there could be elements of $B$ entirely outside $g$'s range, as long as $f$ still reaches every element of $C$ through the range $g$ does cover), nor does $g$ need to be one-to-one (multiple elements of $A$ could map to the same element of $B$). A simple counterexample confirms it: let $B=\{1,2\}$, $C=\{1\}$, $f$ onto, and $g$ mapping every element of $A$ to just $1\in B$ — $g$ is neither onto nor one-to-one, yet $f\circ g$ is trivially onto.

go:460072.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 8
go:460072.question:
Let $G$ be any undirected graph with positive edge weights, and $T$ be a minimum spanning tree of $G$. For any two vertices, $u$ and $v$, let $d_{1}(u, v)$ and $d_{2}(u, v)$ be the shortest distances between $u$ and $v$ in $G$ and $T$, respectively. Which ONE of the options is CORRECT for all possible $G, T, u$ and $v$ ?

  1. $d_{1}(u, v)=d_{2}(u, v)$
  2. $d_{1}(u, v) \leq d_{2}(u, v)$
  3. $d_{1}(u, v) \geq d_{2}(u, v)$
  4. $d_{1}(u, v) \neq d_{2}(u, v)$

detailed_solution.markdown: $T$ is a subgraph of $G$ using only a subset of $G$'s edges, so any path that exists inside $T$ between $u$ and $v$ is also a valid path in $G$ (with the exact same total weight). This means the shortest path in $G$ can never be longer than the shortest path in $T$ — $G$ has strictly more routing options available (all of $T$'s edges, plus possibly more), so it can only match or beat $T$'s best distance. So $d_1(u,v)\le d_2(u,v)$ always holds (equality is common but not guaranteed — a shortcut through a non-tree edge in $G$ can make $d_1$ strictly smaller).

go:460071.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 9
go:460071.question:
Consider the following context-free grammar $G$, where $S, A$, and $B$ are the variables (non-terminals), $a$ and $b$ are the terminal symbols, $S$ is the start variable, and the rules of $G$ are described as:
$$ \begin{array}{l} S \rightarrow a a B \mid A b b \\ A \rightarrow a \mid a A \\ B \rightarrow b \mid b B \end{array}$$
Which ONE of the languages $L(G)$ is accepted by $G$ ?

  1. $L(G)=\left\{a^{2} b^{n} \mid n \geq 1\right\} \cup\left\{a^{n} b^{2} \mid n \geq 1\right\}$
  2. $L(G)=\left\{a^{n} b^{2 n} \mid n \geq 1\right\} \cup\left\{a^{2 n} b^{n} \mid n \geq 1\right\}$
  3. $L(G)=\left\{a^{n} b^{n} \mid n \geq 1\right\}$
  4. $L(G)=\left\{a^{2 n} b^{2 n} \mid n \geq 1\right\}$

detailed_solution.markdown:
$A\to a\mid aA$ generates exactly the strings $a^n$ for $n\ge1$ (one or more $a$'s), and similarly $B\to b\mid bB$ generates $b^n$ for $n\ge1$.

So:

- $S\to aaB$ generates $aa$ followed by $b^n$ ($n\ge1$), i.e. the set $\{a^2b^n\mid n\ge1\}$.

- $S\to Abb$ generates $a^n$ ($n\ge1$) followed by $bb$, i.e. the set $\{a^nb^2\mid n\ge1\}$.

$L(G)$ is the union of these two alternatives.

go:460070.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 10
go:460070.question:
Consider the following recurrence relation:
$$ T(n)=2 T(n-1)+n 2^{n} \text { for } n>0, \quad T(0)=1$$

Which ONE of the following options is CORRECT?

  1. $T(n)=\Theta\left(n^{2} 2^{n}\right)$
  2. $T(n)=\Theta\left(n 2^{n}\right)$
  3. $T(n)=\Theta\left((\log n)^{2} 2^{n}\right)$
  4. $T(n)=\Theta\left(4^{n}\right)$

detailed_solution.markdown:
$T(n)=2T(n-1)+n2^n$. Substitute $T(n)=2^nS(n)$:

$2^nS(n)=2\cdot2^{n-1}S(n-1)+n2^n=2^nS(n-1)+n2^n$

Dividing through by $2^n$: $S(n)=S(n-1)+n$.

Unrolling this simple recurrence: $$S(n)=S(0)+\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}k=1+\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}=\Theta(n^2)$$.

So $T(n)=2^n\cdot\Theta(n^2)=\Theta(n^22^n)$.

go:460069.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 11
go:460069.question:
Consider the following $B^{+}$tree with $5$ nodes, in which a node can store at most $3$ key values The value $23$ is now inserted in the $B^{+}$tree. Which of the following options(s) is/are CORRECT?

  1. None of the nodes will split.
  2. At least one node will split and redistribute.
  3. The total number of nodes will remain same.
  4. The height of the tree will increase.

detailed_solution.markdown: Inserting a new key into a $B^+$ tree always follows the same pattern: search down to the correct leaf, insert the key there in sorted order, and if that leaf now holds more than the maximum allowed keys (here, more than $3$), it must split into two leaves, pushing/copying up a separator key into the parent. Since the target leaf here is already at its maximum capacity of $3$ keys before inserting $23$, it overflows and must split; this new separator key then gets inserted into the parent node, which can itself overflow and split further, potentially propagating all the way up to a new root. Whenever a split reaches (or creates a new) root, the height of the tree increases by one level. Splitting always increases the total node count (a leaf becomes two, or an internal node splits into two) — it never leaves the count unchanged, and "no node splits" is only possible if the target leaf had spare capacity, which it did not here.

go:460068.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 12
go:460068.question:
Consider the $3$-way handshaking protocol for TCP connection establishment. Let the three packets exchanged during the connection establishment be denoted as $\text{P1, P2}$, and $\text{P3}$, in order. Which of the following option(s) is/are TRUE with respect to TCP header flags that are set in the packets?

  1. $\mathrm{P} 3: \mathrm{SYN}=1, \mathrm{ACK}=1$
  2. $\mathrm{P} 2: \mathrm{SYN}=1, \mathrm{ACK}=1$
  3. $\text{P2}$: $\mathrm{SYN}=0, \mathrm{ACK}=1$
  4. $\text{P1: SYN = 1}$

detailed_solution.markdown: TCP's 3-way handshake, packet by packet: - P1 (client → server): the client initiates with SYN=1 (and ACK=0, since there's nothing to acknowledge yet). - P2 (server → client): the server both acknowledges the client's SYN and sends its own SYN, so SYN=1, ACK=1 simultaneously (this combined SYN-ACK packet is the hallmark of TCP's handshake). - P3 (client → server): the client only needs to acknowledge the server's SYN, so SYN=0, ACK=1 (not SYN=1,ACK=1 as one distractor suggests). So the correct flags are P1: SYN=1, and P2: SYN=1 & ACK=1.

go:460067.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 13
go:460067.question:
Consider the given system of linear equations for variables $x$ and $y$, where $k$ is a real-valued constant. Which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?
$$ \begin{array}{l} x+k y=1 \\ k x+y=-1 \end{array} $$

  1. There is exactly one value of $k$ for which the above system of equations has no solution.
  2. There exist an infinite number of values of $k$ for which the system of equations has no solution.
  3. There exists exactly one value of $k$ for which the system of equations has exactly one solution.
  4. There exists exactly one value of $k$ for which the system of equations has an infinite number of solutions.

options.label: A
options.text: There is exactly one value of $ for which the above system of equations has no solution.
options.html: There is exactly one value of $ for which the above system of equations has no solution.

options.label: B
options.text: There exist an infinite number of values of $ for which the system of equations has no solution.
options.html: There exist an infinite number of values of $ for which the system of equations has no solution.

options.label: C
options.text: There exists exactly one value of $ for which the system of equations has exactly one solution.
options.html: There exists exactly one value of $ for which the system of equations has exactly one solution.

options.label: D
options.text: There exists exactly one value of $ for which the system of equations has an infinite number of solutions.
options.html: There exists exactly one value of $ for which the system of equations has an infinite number of solutions.

detailed_solution.markdown: $$\begin{cases}x+ky=1\\kx+y=-1\end{cases}$$, with determinant $\Delta=1-k^2$. No solution requires $\Delta=0$ (i.e. $k=\pm1$) and the two equations to actually be inconsistent (parallel but not identical lines): - $k=1$: equations become $x+y=1$ and $x+y=-1$ — parallel, contradictory → no solution. - $k=-1$: equations become $x-y=1$ and $-x+y=-1$, which is just the first equation multiplied by $-1$ — the same line → infinitely many solutions, not "no solution." So there is exactly one value of $k$ (namely $k=1$) giving no solution, and exactly one value of $k$ (namely $k=-1$) giving infinitely many solutions. For every other $k$ (i.e. $k\ne\pm1$), $\Delta\ne0$ and there's a unique solution — but that happens for infinitely many values of $k$, not just one, so the "exactly one k gives a unique solution" claim is false.

go:460066.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 14
go:460066.question:
Let $X$ be a $3$-variable Boolean function that produces output as $'1'$ when at least two of the input variables are $'1'$. Which of the following statement(s) is/are CORRECT, where $a, b, c, d, e$ are Boolean variables?

  1. $X(a, b, X(c, d, e))=X(X(a, b, c), d, e)$
  2. $X(a, b, X(a, b, c))=X(a, b, c)$
  3. $X(a, b, X(a, c, d))=(X(a, b, a)$ AND $X(c, d, c))$
  4. $X(a, b, c)=X(a, X(a, b, c), X(a, c, c))$

detailed_solution.markdown: $X$ is the 3-input majority function: $X(p,q,r)=1$ iff at least $2$ of $p,q,r$ are $1$. A useful fact: whenever two of the three inputs to $X$ are the same variable $v$, the output is forced to equal $v$ regardless of the third input (e.g. $X(v,v,\text{anything})=v$). Checking $X(a,b,X(a,b,c))=X(a,b,c)$: let $m=X(a,b,c)$. If $a=b$, then $m=a$ too, and $X(a,b,m)=X(a,a,a)=a=m$. If $a\ne b$, then (since one of $a,b$ is $0$ and the other $1$) $m=c$, and $X(a,b,m)=X(a,b,c)=m$. Either way it checks out. True. Checking $X(a,b,c)=X(a,X(a,b,c),X(a,c,c))$: note $X(a,c,c)=c$ (two matching inputs). Let $m=X(a,b,c)$. If $a=b$: $m=a$, and $X(a,m,c)=X(a,a,c)=a=m$. If $a\ne b$: $m=c$, and $X(a,m,c)=X(a,c,c)=c=m$. Checks out both ways. True. The other two options can be shown false with a direct counterexample assignment of $a,b,c,d$ (the two sides disagree for some input combination) — they do not hold as general identities.

go:460065.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 15
go:460065.question:
The number $-6$ can be represented as $1010$ in $4$-bit $2$'s complement representation. Which of the following is/are CORRECT $2$ 's complement representation(s) of $-6$?

  1. $1000 \: 1010$ in $8$ -bits
  2. $1111 \: 1010$ in $8$-bits
  3. $1000 \: 0000 \: 0000 \:1010$ in $16$-bits
  4. $1111 \: 1111 \: 1111 \: 1010$ in $16$-bits

detailed_solution.markdown: Correctly extending a two's-complement number to more bits requires sign-extension: replicate the sign bit (here, the leading $1$, since $-6$ is negative) into all the new higher-order bit positions — you cannot just prepend arbitrary/zero bits. $-6$ in 4-bit: $1010$. Correct 8-bit sign-extension: $1111\,1010$ (four $1$'s prepended). The alternative $1000\,1010$ incorrectly prepends $1000$ instead of replicating the sign bit — wrong. Correct 16-bit sign-extension: $1111\,1111\,1111\,1010$ (twelve $1$'s prepended). The alternative $1000\,0000\,0000\,1010$ is similarly wrong.

go:460064.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 16
go:460064.question:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE for any binary search tree (BST) having $n$ distinct integers?

  1. The maximum length of a path from the root node to any other node is $(n-1)$.
  2. An inorder traversal will always produce a sorted sequence of elements.
  3. Finding an element takes $O\left(\log _{2} n\right)$ time in the worst case.
  4. Every BST is also a Min-Heap.

detailed_solution.markdown: Checking each BST claim for $n$ distinct integers: - Maximum path length from root to any node is $n-1$: true — in the worst case (a completely skewed/degenerate BST, essentially a linked list), all $n$ nodes form a single chain, giving a root-to-deepest-node path of $n-1$ edges, which is also the largest this can ever be since there are only $n$ nodes total. - Inorder traversal always produces sorted order: true — this is the defining property of a BST (left subtree $<$ node $<$ right subtree, recursively), and it holds regardless of the tree's shape. - Finding an element takes $O(\log_2n)$ time in the worst case: false — that bound only holds for a balanced BST. A skewed/degenerate BST (as noted above) can force search time all the way up to $O(n)$. - Every BST is also a Min-Heap: false — a min-heap requires every parent to be smaller than both children, but a BST only orders left $<$ parent $<$ right; nothing stops a BST's left child from being smaller than its grandparent in ways that violate heap order.

go:460063.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 17
go:460063.question:
A partial data path of a processor is given in the figure, where $\text{RA, RB,}$ and $\text{RZ}$ are $32$-bit registers. Which option(s) is/are CORRECT related to arithmetic operations using the data path as shown?

 

  1. The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving two registers.
  2. The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving one register and one immediate value.
  3. The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving two immediate values.
  4. The data path can only implement arithmetic operations involving one register and one immediate value.

detailed_solution.markdown:
The given data path consists of: - Two 32-bit registers: RA and RB. - Two multiplexers (Mux_A and Mux_B). - Each multiplexer can select either: - the corresponding register value, or - a 32-bit immediate value. - The selected inputs are fed to the ALU, whose output is stored in register RZ. Thus, the ALU can receive the following combinations of operands:
Mux_A Mux_B Operands
RA RB Two registers
RA Immediate One register + one immediate
Immediate RB One immediate + one register
Immediate Immediate Two immediate values
Now, evaluate each statement. Option A: The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving two registers. Since Mux_A can select RA and Mux_B can select RB, the ALU can perform operations such as $RZ \leftarrow RA + RB$ Hence, Option A is Correct. Option B: The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving one register and one immediate value. Examples: $RZ \leftarrow RA + 10$ or $RZ \leftarrow 20 + RB$ Therefore, Option B is Correct. Option C: The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving two immediate values. Both multiplexers can independently select their immediate inputs. Therefore, the ALU can perform operations like $RZ \leftarrow 15 + 25$ Hence, Option C is Correct. Option D: The data path can only implement arithmetic operations involving one register and one immediate value. This is false because the data path also supports: - Register + Register - Immediate + Immediate - Register + Immediate Therefore, Option D is Incorrect.

go:460062.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 18
go:460062.question:
A regular language $L$ is accepted by a non-deterministic finite automaton (NFA) with $n$ states. Which of the following statement(s) is/are FALSE?

  1. $L$ may have an accepting NFA with $< n$ states.
  2. $L$ may have an accepting DFA with $<n$ states.
  3. There exists a DFA with $\leq 2^{n}$ states that accepts $L$.
  4. Every DFA that accepts $L$ has $>2^{n}$ states.

detailed_solution.markdown: For a regular language $L$ accepted by some $n$-state NFA, recall two standard facts: (1) subset construction always produces an equivalent DFA with at most $2^n$ states, and (2) NFA/DFA state counts for a given language are not unique — smaller equivalent automata can certainly exist. - "$L$ may have an accepting NFA with $< n$ states": could well be true (this $n$-state NFA might not be minimal), so calling it FALSE is incorrect — it's a true possibility, not a false statement. - "$L$ may have an accepting DFA with $< n$ states": also entirely possible depending on the language, so this is also true (not false). - "There exists a DFA with $\le 2^n$ states accepting $L$": guaranteed true by subset construction — so this is also true, not false. - "Every DFA that accepts L has $> 2^n$ states": this directly contradicts the subset-construction guarantee (a DFA with at most $2^n$ states always exists) — so this statement is definitely FALSE.

go:460061.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 19
go:460061.question:
Suppose in a multiprogramming environment, the following C program segment is executed. A process goes into I/O queue whenever an I/O related operation is performed. Assume that there will always be a context switch whenever a process requests for an I/O, and also whenever the process returns from an I/O. The number of times the process will enter the ready queue during its lifetime (not counting the time the process enters the ready queue when it is run initially) is ___________ . Answer in integer)

int main
{
int x=0,i=0;
scanf("%d",&x);
for(i=0; i<20; i++)
{
x = x+20;
printf("%d\n",x);
}
return 0;
}

detailed_solution.markdown: Every time the process performs an I/O operation, it leaves the CPU (context switch out to the I/O queue) and, once the I/O completes, must re-enter the ready queue to wait for the CPU again (context switch back). Counting the I/O operations in this program: one $\text{scanf}$ at the start, plus one $\text{printf}$ inside each of the $20$ loop iterations — that's $1+20=21$ I/O operations in total. Each of these $21$ I/O completions causes exactly one re-entry into the ready queue (and we're told not to count the very first, initial dispatch into the ready queue separately, which is consistent with this count already excluding it).

go:460060.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 20
go:460060.question: Let $\text{S}$ be the set of all ternary strings defined over the alphabet $\{a, b, c\}$. Consider all strings in $\text{S}$ that contain at least one occurrence of two consecutive symbols, that is, $\text{"aa"}$, $\text{"bb"}$ or $\text{"cc"}$. The number of such strings of length $5$ that are possible is __________. (Answer in integer).

detailed_solution.markdown: Total ternary strings of length $5$ over $\{a,b,c\}$: $3^5=243$. It's easier to count the complement: strings with no two consecutive equal symbols anywhere. The first symbol has $3$ choices; each subsequent symbol just needs to differ from its immediate predecessor, giving $2$ choices each time: $3\times2^4=3\times16=48$ such "no-repeat" strings. So strings containing at least one consecutive repeat $=243-48=195$.

go:460059.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 21
go:460059.question:
Consider the given function $f(x)$.

$$f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
a x+b & \text { for } x<1 \\
x^{3}+x^{2}+1 & \text { for } x \geq 1
\end{array}\right.
$$
If the function is differentiable everywhere, the value of $b$ must be ________. (rounded off to one decimal place)

detailed_solution.markdown: For $f$ to be differentiable at $x=1$, it must first be continuous there, and then have matching one-sided derivatives. Continuity: left-hand value $=a(1)+b=a+b$; right-hand value $=1^3+1^2+1=3$. So $a+b=3$. Matching derivatives: left derivative $=\dfrac{d}{dx}(ax+b)=a$. Right derivative $=\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^3+x^2+1)=3x^2+2x$, evaluated at $x=1$: $3+2=5$. So $a=5$. Substituting back: $b=3-a=3-5=-2$.

go:460058.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 22
go:460058.question: A box contains $5$ coins: $4$ regular coins and $1$ fake coin. When a regular coin is tossed, the probability $P($ head $)=0.5$ and for a fake coin, $P($ head $)=1$. You pick a coin at random and toss it twice, and get two heads. The probability that the coin you have chosen is the fake coin is __________. (rounded off to two decimal places)

detailed_solution.markdown:
By Bayes' theorem, $P(\text{fake}\mid HH)=\dfrac{P(HH\mid\text{fake})P(\text{fake})}{P(HH)}$.

$P(HH\mid\text{fake})=1\times1=1$ (fake coin always shows heads). $P(HH\mid\text{regular})=0.5\times0.5=0.25$.

$P(\text{fake})=\dfrac15$, $P(\text{regular})=\dfrac45$.

$P(HH)=1\times\dfrac15+0.25\times\dfrac45=0.2+0.2=0.4$.

$P(\text{fake}\mid HH)=\dfrac{0.2}{0.4}=0.5$.

go:460057.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 23
go:460057.question:
The pseudocode of a function $\text{fun }$ is given below:
 

fun(int A[0,....,n-1]) {
for i=0 to n-2
for j=0 to n-i-2
if (A[j]>A[j+1])
then swap A[j] and A[j+1]
}

Let $A[0, \ldots, 29]$ be an array storing $30$ distinct integers in descending order. The number of swap operations that will be performed, if the function $\text{fun }$ is called with $A[0, \ldots, 29]$ as argument, is _________. (Answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown: This is exactly the standard bubble-sort pseudocode. On a fully descending-order array, every single adjacent-pair comparison across the entire double loop finds the pair out of order, so a swap happens on every comparison — there are no comparisons at all that skip the swap. Total comparisons (and hence swaps) $$=\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{n-2}(n-1-i)=\binom{n}{2}$$ for an $n$-element array. With $n=30$: $\binom{30}{2}=\dfrac{30\times29}{2}=435$.

go:460056.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 24
go:460056.question:
#include <stdio.h>
void foo(int *p, int x) {
*p=x;
}
int main{
int *z;
int a = 20, b = 25;
z = &a;
foo(z,b);
printf("%d",a);
return 0;
}

The output of the given $\text{C}$ program is __________. (Answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown:
$\text{z}=\&\text{a}$ makes $z$ point to $a$ (currently $20$).

$\text{foo(z, b)}$ passes $z$ (the address of $a$) and $b$'s value ($25$) into $\text{foo(int *p, int x)}$, so inside $\text{foo}$, $p$ points to $a$ and $x=25$.

${*}\text{p}=\text{x}$ writes $25$ into whatever $p$ points to — i.e. directly into $a$ itself (since pointers give real access to the caller's variable). So $a$ becomes $25$.

$\text{printf}$ then prints the now-updated $a$.

go:460055.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 25
go:460055.question:
The height of any rooted tree is defined as the maximum number of edges in the path from the root node to any leaf node.

Suppose a Min-Heap $\text{T}$ stores $32$ keys. The height of $\text{T}$ is ___________. (Answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown: A min-heap with $N$ keys is stored as a nearly-complete binary tree, and its height (max edges from root to a leaf) is $\lfloor\log_2N\rfloor$. Level $0$ holds $1$ node, level $1$ holds $2$, level $2$ holds $4$, level $3$ holds $8$, level $4$ holds $16$ — cumulatively $1+2+4+8+16=31$ nodes fill levels $0$ through $4$ completely. The $32$nd key must then start a new level, level 5.

go:460054.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 26
go:460054.question:
Consider a memory system with $1 \mathrm{M}$ bytes of main memory and $16 \mathrm{~K}$ bytes of cache memory. Assume that the processor generates $20$-bit memory address, and the cache block size is $16$ bytes. If the cache uses direct mapping, how many bits will be required to store all the $\operatorname{tag}$ values? [Assume memory is byte addressable, $1 \mathrm{~K}=2^{10}$, $1 \mathrm{M}=2^{20}$.]

  1. $6 \times 2^{10}$
  2. $8 \times 2^{10}$
  3. $2^{12}$
  4. $2^{14}$

detailed_solution.markdown: Cache $=16\text{K}=2^{14}$ bytes, block size $=16=2^4$ bytes, so number of cache lines $=\dfrac{2^{14}}{2^4}=2^{10}$ — index field $=10$ bits, offset field $=4$ bits. Main memory $=1\text{M}=2^{20}$ bytes, byte-addressable, so the address is $20$ bits wide. Tag field $=20-10-4=6$ bits per line. Total bits needed to store all tag values $=6\text{ bits}\times2^{10}\text{ lines}=6\times2^{10}$.

go:460053.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 27
go:460053.question:
A processor has $64$ general-purpose registers and $50$ distinct instruction types. An instruction is encoded in $32$-bits. What is the maximum number of bits that can be used to store the immediate operand for the given instruction?

$\text{ADD R1}$, $\#25$  / /  $\text{R 1=R 1+25}$

  1. $16$
  2. $20$
  3. $22$
  4. $24$

detailed_solution.markdown: With $64=2^6$ registers, each register-number field needs $6$ bits. With $50$ distinct instruction types, the opcode field needs $\lceil\log_2 50\rceil=6$ bits (since $2^5=32<50\le64=2^6$). The instruction $\text{ADD R1, \#25}$ (meaning $\text{R1}=\text{R1}+25$) only needs to name one register (used as both source and destination), plus an immediate value. So the $32$-bit instruction splits as: opcode ($6$ bits) $+$ one register field ($6$ bits) $+$ immediate field (the rest). Immediate field width $=32-6-6=20$ bits.

go:460052.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 28
go:460052.question:
A computer has two processors, $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$. Four processes $P_{1}, P_{2}, P_{3}, P_{4}$ with CPU bursts of $20,16,25$, and $10$ milliseconds, respectively, arrive at the same time and these are the only processes in the system. The scheduler uses non-preemptive priority scheduling, with priorities decided as follows:

  • $M_{1}$ uses priority of execution for the processes as, $P_{1}>P_{3}>P_{2}>P_{4}$, i.e., $P_{1}$ and $P_{4}$ have highest and lowest priorities, respectively.
  • $M_{2}$ uses priority of execution for the processes as, $P_{2}>P_{3}>P_{4}>P_{1}$, i.e., $P_{2}$ and $P_{1}$ have highest and lowest priorities, respectively.

A process $P_{i}$ is scheduled to a processor $M_{k}$, if the processor is free and no other process $P_{j}$ is waiting with higher priority. At any given point of time, a process can be allocated to any one of the free processors without violating the execution priority rules. Ignore the context switch time. What will be the average waiting time of the processes in milliseconds?

  1. $9.00$
  2. $8.75$
  3. $6.50$
  4. $7.50$

detailed_solution.markdown: All four processes arrive together at $t=0$ with two free processors, so two of them start immediately. Since $P_1$ is $M_1$'s top priority and $P_2$ is $M_2$'s top priority (and conveniently each is the other machine's lowest priority, so there's no conflict), the natural non-conflicting start is $P_1\to M_1$ and $P_2\to M_2$, both beginning at $t=0$. $P_2$ (burst $16$) finishes first, at $t=16$, freeing $M_2$. Among the still-waiting $P_3,P_4$, $M_2$'s priority order ($P_2{>}P_3{>}P_4{>}P_1$) favors $P_3$, so $P_3$ starts on $M_2$ at $t=16$, running until $16+25=41$. $P_1$ (burst $20$) finishes next, at $t=20$, freeing $M_1$. Only $P_4$ remains waiting, so it starts on $M_1$ at $t=20$, running until $20+10=30$. Waiting times: $P_1{:}\,0$, $P_2{:}\,0$, $P_3{:}\,16-0=16$, $P_4{:}\,20-0=20$. Average $=\dfrac{0+0+16+20}{4}=\dfrac{36}{4}=9$.

go:460051.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 29
go:460051.question:
Consider two relations describing teams and players in a sports league:

  • teams(tid, tname): tid, tname are team-id and team-name, respectively
  • players(pid,pname,tid): pid, pname, and tid denote player-id, playername and the team-id of the player, respectively

Which ONE of the following tuple relational calculus queries returns the name of the players who play for the team having tname as ' $M I^{\prime}$ ?

  1. $\left\{p\right.$. pname $\mid p \in$ players $\wedge \exists t\left(t \in\right.$ teams $\left.\left.\wedge p . t i d=t . t i d \wedge t . t n a m e=' M I^{\prime}\right)\right\}$
  2. $\left\{p\right.$. pname $\mid p \in$ teams $\wedge \exists t\left(t \in\right.$ players $\left.\left.\wedge p . t i d=t . t i d \wedge t . t n a m e=' M I^{\prime}\right)\right\}$
  3. $\left\{p\right.$. pname $\mid p \in$ players $\wedge \exists t\left(t \in\right.$ teams $\wedge t$. tname $\left.\left.=' M I^{\prime}\right)\right\}$
  4. $\left\{p\right.$. pname $\mid p \in$ teams $\wedge \exists t\left(t \in\right.$ players $\wedge t$. tname $\left.\left.=' M I^{\prime}\right)\right\}$

detailed_solution.markdown:
We want, for each player $p$ in $\text{players}$, their name, restricted to only those players whose $tid$ matches some team $t$ in $\text{teams}$ with $t.tname=\text{'MI'}$.

This is exactly:

$\{p.pname\mid p\in players\ \wedge\ \exists t(t\in teams\ \wedge\ p.tid=t.tid\ \wedge\ t.tname=\text{'MI'})\}$

The key correctness checks: the outer variable $p$ must range over $players$ (not $teams$, since we want player names), and the join condition $p.tid=t.tid$ must actually be present inside the existential (options that drop this join condition would incorrectly return every player's name whenever team 'MI' exists at all, regardless of which team the player is actually on).

go:460050.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 30
go:460050.question:
A packet with the destination $\text{IP}$ address $145.36 .109 .70$ arrives at a router whose routing table is shown. Which interface will the packet be forwarded to?

$$\begin{array}{|l|l|l|} \hline \textbf{Subnet Address} & \textbf{Subnet Mask ( in CIDR notation)} & \textbf{Interface} \\ \hline 145.36.0.0 & /16 & E1 \\ \hline 145.36.128.0 & /17 & E2 \\ \hline 145.36.64.0 & /18 & E3 \\ \hline 145.36.255.0 & /24 & E4 \\ \hline \text{Default} & - & E5 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

  1. $\text{E3}$
  2. $\text{E1}$
  3. $\text{E2}$
  4. $\text{E5}$

detailed_solution.markdown: Routers use longest-prefix matching: find every subnet entry that contains the destination address, and among those, forward via the one with the most specific (longest) prefix. Destination: $145.36.109.70$. Check each entry: - $145.36.0.0/16$ (E1): matches any $145.36.x.x$ — matches. - $145.36.128.0/17$ (E2): covers 3rd octet $128$-$255$; our 3rd octet is $109$ — no match. - $145.36.64.0/18$ (E3): covers 3rd octet $64$-$127$; $109$ falls in this range — matches. - $145.36.255.0/24$ (E4): only $145.36.255.x$; no match. Between the two matches (E1's $/16$ and E3's $/18$), the $/18$ is more specific (longer prefix), so it wins.

go:460049.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 31
go:460049.question:
Let $A$ be a $2 \times 2$ matrix as given.
$$ A=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{array}\right]$$

What are the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^{13}$ ?

  1. $1,-1$
  2. $2 \sqrt{2},-2 \sqrt{2}$
  3. $4 \sqrt{2},-4 \sqrt{2}$
  4. $64 \sqrt{2},-64 \sqrt{2}$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Find the eigenvalues of $$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}$$ from its characteristic equation:

$(1-\lambda)(-1-\lambda)-1\times1=0\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda^2-1-1=0\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda^2=2\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda=\pm\sqrt2$

If $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$, then $\lambda^{13}$ is the corresponding eigenvalue of $A^{13}$ (eigenvalues of a matrix power are just the original eigenvalues raised to that power):

$(\sqrt2)^{13}=2^{13/2}=2^{6}\cdot2^{1/2}=64\sqrt2$, and similarly $(-\sqrt2)^{13}=-64\sqrt2$.

go:460048.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 32
go:460048.question:
Consider the following four variable Boolean function in sum-of-product form

$$ F\left(b_{3}, b_{2}, b_{1}, b_{0}\right)=\sum(0,2,4,8,10,11,12)$$

where the value of the function is computed by considering $b_{3} b_{2} b_{1} b_{0}$ as a $4$-bit binary number, where $b_{3}$ denotes the most significant bit and $b_{0}$ denotes the least significant bit. Note that there are no don't care terms. Which ONE of the following options is the CORRECT minimized Boolean expression for $F$ ?

  1. $\bar{b}_{1} \bar{b}_{0}+\bar{b}_{2} \bar{b}_{0}+b_{1} \bar{b}_{2} b_{3}$
  2. $\bar{b}_{1} \bar{b}_{0}+\bar{b}_{2} \bar{b}_{0}$
  3. $\bar{b}_{2} \bar{b}_{0}+b_{1} b_{2} b_{3}$
  4. $\bar{b}_{0} \bar{b}_{2}+\bar{b}_{3}$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Plotting $F(b_3,b_2,b_1,b_0)=\sum(0,2,4,8,10,11,12)$ on a K-map and grouping adjacent $1$s:

- $\bar b_1\bar b_0$ covers minterms where $b_1{=}0,b_0{=}0$: $0,2,8,10$

- $\bar b_2\bar b_0$ covers minterms where $b_2{=}0,b_0{=}0$: $0,4,8,12$

- $b_1\bar b_2b_3$ covers minterms where $b_3{=}1,b_2{=}0,b_1{=}1$: $10,11$

Union of these three terms $=\{0,2,4,8,10,11,12\}$ exactly — matching the target minterm list precisely, with no extra minterms picked up. Each term is also a necessary, non-redundant group (removing any one leaves some minterm uncovered), so this is the minimal SOP form.

go:460047.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 33
go:460047.question:
Let $G(V, E)$ be an undirected and unweighted graph with $100$ vertices. Let $d(u, v)$ denote the number of edges in a shortest path between vertices $u$ and $v$ in $V$. Let the maximum value of $d(u, v), u, v \in V$ such that $u \neq v$, be $30$. Let $T$ be any breadth-first-search tree of $G$. Which ONE of the given options is CORRECT for every such graph $G$ ?

  1. The height of $T$ is exactly $15$.
  2. The height of $T$ is exactly $30$.
  3. The height of $T$ is at least $15$.
  4. The height of $T$ is at least $30$.

detailed_solution.markdown: Let the diameter of the graph be the maximum shortest distance between any two vertices. It is given that $\max_{u,v\in V,\;u\ne v} d(u,v)=30.$ Thus, the diameter of the graph is 30. Relation between BFS Tree Height and Graph Diameter A Breadth-First Search (BFS) tree rooted at a vertex (r) has the following property: - The level of every vertex equals its shortest distance from the root. - Therefore, the height of the BFS tree is the maximum shortest distance from the root to any vertex, which is called the eccentricity of the root. Let the height of the BFS tree be (h). Then, $h=\max_{v\in V} d(r,v).$ Using the Diameter Let the diameter of the graph be (D=30). A well-known property of graphs is $\text{Radius} \ge \left\lceil\frac{D}{2}\right\rceil.$ Since $D=30,$ we get $\left\lceil\frac{30}{2}\right\rceil=15.$ Every vertex has eccentricity at least the radius. Hence, regardless of the chosen BFS root, $h\ge 15.$ The height need not be exactly 15 or exactly 30. It can be any value between 15 and 30 depending on the chosen root. For example: - If the BFS starts from a central vertex, the height can be 15. - If it starts from an end vertex of a diameter, the height can be 30. Correct Answer: (C) The height of (T) is at least 15.

go:460046.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 34
go:460046.question:
Consider the following two languages over the alphabet $\{a, b\}$:

$$\begin{array}{l} L_{1}=\left\{\alpha \beta \alpha \mid \alpha \in\{a, b\}^{+} \text {AND } \beta \in\{a, b\}^{+}\right\} \\ L_{2}=\left\{\alpha \beta \alpha \mid \alpha \in\{a\}^{+} \text {AND } \beta \in\{a, b\}^{+}\right\}
\end{array}$$

Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT?

  1. Both $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ are regular languages.
  2. $L_{1}$ is a regular language but $L_{2}$ is not a regular language.
  3. $L_{1}$ is not a regular language but $L_{2}$ is a regular language.
  4. Neither $L_{1}$ nor $L_{2}$ is a regular language.

detailed_solution.markdown: $L_1=\{\alpha\beta\alpha\mid\alpha,\beta\in\{a,b\}^+\}$ (α completely unrestricted): checking membership genuinely requires comparing an arbitrary-length prefix against an arbitrary-length suffix for exact equality. For instance, "$abbaab$" is in $L_1$ (via $\alpha=ab,\beta=ba$) even though its very first and very last characters differ — so no bounded "look at a few characters" trick works; a finite automaton cannot carry the unbounded memory needed to remember an arbitrarily long prefix for later comparison. This is the same style of argument used to show languages like $\{ww\}$ are non-regular. $L_1$ is not regular. $L_2=\{\alpha\beta\alpha\mid\alpha\in\{a\}^+,\beta\in\{a,b\}^+\}$ (α restricted to all-a's): here, since $\alpha$ consists only of $a$'s, we can always just use the shortest valid split ($|\alpha|=1$): any string of length $\ge3$ that starts with $a$ and ends with $a$ can always be decomposed as (first character $a$) + (everything in between, as $\beta$) + (last character $a$). So $L_2$ is exactly "strings of length $\ge3$ starting and ending with $a$," which is simply matched by the regular expression $a(a|b)^+a$. $L_2$ is regular.

go:460045.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 35
go:460045.question:
Consider the following two languages over the alphabet $\{a, b, c\}$, where $m$ and $n$ are natural numbers.

$$\begin{aligned} L_{1} & =\left\{a^{m} b^{m} c^{m+n} \mid m, n \geq 1\right\} \\ L_{2} & =\left\{a^{m} b^{n} c^{m+n} \mid m, n \geq 1\right\} \end{aligned}$$

Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT?

  1. Both $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ are context-free languages.
  2. $L_{1}$ is a context-free language but $L_{2}$ is not a context-free language.
  3. $L_{1}$ is not a context-free language but $L_{2}$ is a context-free language.
  4. Neither $L_{1}$ nor $L_{2}$ are context-free languages.

detailed_solution.markdown: $L_1=\{a^mb^mc^{m+n}\mid m,n\ge1\}$: this requires two separate comparisons tied to the same value $m$ — matching $a$'s against $b$'s exactly (using up a stack), and independently comparing the $c$-count against that same $m$ again. A single-stack PDA can only "remember and compare" one running count at a time; once the stack is used up matching $a$'s against $b$'s, the value of $m$ is no longer available to compare against the $c$'s. This mirrors the classic non-context-free pattern $a^nb^nc^n$. $L_1$ is not context-free. $L_2=\{a^mb^nc^{m+n}\mid m,n\ge1\}$: here the $c$-count only needs to match the combined total of $a$'s and $b$'s (not two separate comparisons). A single stack handles this easily: push one symbol for every $a$ and every $b$ (treating them the same way), then pop one symbol per $c$, accepting if the stack empties exactly when the input ends. $L_2$ is context-free.

go:460044.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 36
go:460044.question:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE while computing $\operatorname{First}$ and $\operatorname{Follow}$ during top down parsing by a compiler?

  1. For a production $A \rightarrow \epsilon, \epsilon$ will be added to $\operatorname{First}(A)$.
  2. If there is any input right end marker, it will be added to $\text{First(S)}$, where $S$ is the start symbol.
  3. For a production $A \rightarrow \epsilon, \epsilon$ will be added to Follow $\text{(A)}$.
  4. If there is any input right end marker, it will be added to $\operatorname{Follow}(S)$, where $\text{S}$ is the start symbol.

detailed_solution.markdown: Standard rules for computing $\text{First}$ and $\text{Follow}$ sets: - "For $A\to\epsilon$, add $\epsilon$ to First(A)": TRUE — this is exactly the base rule for handling nullable productions in First-set computation. - "If there's an input right-end marker, add it to First(S)": FALSE — the end marker $\$$ belongs in $\text{Follow}$ sets (marking "nothing more can follow"), never in a $\text{First}$ set. - "For $A\to\epsilon$, add $\epsilon$ to Follow(A)": FALSE — $\epsilon$ is never placed into any $\text{Follow}$ set; $\text{Follow}$ sets only ever contain actual terminals (and possibly $\$$). - "If there's an input right-end marker, add it to Follow(S)": TRUE — this is the standard initialization rule, since nothing legitimately follows the start symbol except the end of input.

go:460043.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 37
go:460043.question:
Consider a relational schema team $\text{(name,city,owner)}$, with functional dependencies $\{\text{name} \rightarrow \text{city}, \text{name} \rightarrow \text{owner} \}$.

The relation team is decomposed into two relations, $\text{t1(name,city)}$ and $\text{t2(name, owner)}$. Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?

  1. The relation team is NOT in BCNF .
  2. The relations $t 1$ and $t 2$ are in BCNF.
  3. The decomposition constitutes a lossless join.
  4. The relation team is NOT in $3$ NF .

detailed_solution.markdown: $team(name,city,owner)$ with $name\to city,\ name\to owner$. Since $name$ alone functionally determines every other attribute, $name$ is already a candidate key of $team$ — and since every FD's left-hand side ($name$) is already a superkey, $team$ is already in BCNF (and hence also in 3NF) even before decomposing. So both "team is NOT in BCNF" and "team is NOT in 3NF" are false. Decomposing into $t_1(name,city)$ and $t_2(name,owner)$: in each projection, $name$ remains a key (it determines the sole remaining attribute), so both $t_1$ and $t_2$ are trivially in BCNF. True. For losslessness, the common attribute of the decomposition is $name$, and $name\to city$ (i.e. $name$ alone determines all of $t_1$) — satisfying the standard lossless-join test ($R_1\cap R_2$ is a superkey of at least one of the two pieces). True.

go:460042.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 38
go:460042.question:
Which of the following predicate logic formulae/formula is/are CORRECT representation(s) of the statement: "Everyone has exactly one mother"?

The meanings of the predicates used are:

  • mother $(y, x): y$ is the mother of $x$
  • noteq $(x, y): x$ and $y$ are not equal
  1. $ orall x \exists y \exists z(\operatorname{mother}(y, x) \wedge eg \operatorname{mother}(z, x))$
  2. $ orall x \exists y[\operatorname{mother}(y, x) \wedge orall z( \operatorname{noteq} (z, y) ightarrow eg \operatorname{mother} (z, x))]$
  3. $ orall x orall y[\operatorname{mother}(y, x) ightarrow \exists z( \operatorname{mother} (z, x) \wedge eg \operatorname{note} q(z, y))]$
  4. $ orall x \exists y[\operatorname{mother}(y, x) \wedge eg \exists z( \operatorname{note}  q(z, y) \wedge \operatorname{mother} (z, x))]$

detailed_solution.markdown: We want: for every person $x$, there is exactly one $y$ who is $x$'s mother — meaning both existence (someone is the mother) and uniqueness (nobody else also qualifies as a distinct mother). $\forall x\exists y[mother(y,x)\wedge\forall z(noteq(z,y)\to\neg mother(z,x))]$: says "$y$ is a mother of $x$, and every $z$ different from $y$ is not a mother of $x$" — this correctly captures existence plus uniqueness. Correct. $\forall x\exists y[mother(y,x)\wedge\neg\exists z(noteq(z,y)\wedge mother(z,x))]$: by De Morgan's law, $\neg\exists z(noteq(z,y)\wedge mother(z,x))$ is logically identical to $\forall z(noteq(z,y)\to\neg mother(z,x))$ — so this is just a different (but equivalent) way of writing the same correct statement above. Correct. The other two options fail to properly express uniqueness: one only asserts some non-mother exists (too weak, says nothing about all other candidates), and the other is a vacuous implication that never actually forces a mother to exist at all.

go:460041.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 39
go:460041.question:
$A=\{0,1,2,3, \ldots\}$ is the set of non-negative integers. Let $F$ be the set of functions from $A$ to itself. For any two functions, $f_{1}, f_{2} \in \mathrm{~F}$, we define

$$\left(f_{1} \odot f_{2}\right)(n)=f_{1}(n)+f_{2}(n) $$

for every number $n$ in $A$. Which of the following is/are CORRECT about the mathematical structure $(\mathrm{F}, \odot)$ ?

  1. $(\mathrm{F}, \odot)$ is an Abelian group.
  2. $(\mathrm{F}, \odot)$ is an Abelian monoid.
  3. $(F, \odot)$ is a non-Abelian group.
  4. $(\mathrm{F}, \odot)$ is a non-Abelian monoid.

detailed_solution.markdown: $(f_1\odot f_2)(n)=f_1(n)+f_2(n)$ — pointwise addition of functions into the non-negative integers. - Closure: the sum of two non-negative-integer values is still a non-negative integer, so $F$ is closed under $\odot$. - Associativity: inherited directly from ordinary integer addition being associative. - Identity: the constant-zero function $z(n)=0$ satisfies $f\odot z=f$ for every $f$ — an identity element exists. - Commutativity: $f_1(n)+f_2(n)=f_2(n)+f_1(n)$ pointwise, so $\odot$ is commutative. - Inverses: for a general $f$ (e.g. $f(n)=n$), we'd need some $g$ with $f(n)+g(n)=0$, forcing $g(n)=-f(n)$ — but negative values aren't allowed in the codomain $A$. So inverses generally don't exist. Since it's closed, associative, has an identity, and is commutative, but lacks inverses, $(F,\odot)$ is exactly an Abelian monoid (not a group).

go:460040.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 40
go:460040.question:
Consider the following deterministic finite automaton (DFA) defined over the alphabet, $\Sigma=\{a, b\}$. Identify which of the following language(s) is/are accepted by the given DFA.

  1. The set of all strings containing an even number of $b$ 's.
  2. The set of all strings containing the pattern $b a b$.
  3. The set of all strings ending with the pattern $b a b$.
  4. The set of all strings not containing the pattern $a b a$.

detailed_solution.markdown: This DFA, on inspection of its states and transitions, is built to track only the most recently seen $3$ input symbols, entering its unique accepting state precisely when those last three symbols read are exactly "$bab$" — i.e. it's a standard "suffix detector" construction (a small sliding window of recent symbols, accepting whenever that window matches the target pattern at the very end of the input read so far). This is a different (and stricter) condition than merely "contains bab somewhere" (that DFA would need to stay accepting once the pattern is seen, regardless of what comes after, rather than resetting/tracking only the tail) or "even number of b's" or "excludes aba" (which are entirely different acceptance conditions with different structural transitions).

go:460039.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 41
go:460039.question: A disk of size $512 \text{ M}$ bytes is divided into blocks of $64 \text{ K}$ bytes. A file is stored in the disk using linked allocation. In linked allocation, each data block reserves $4$ bytes to store the pointer to the next data block. The link part of the last data block contains a NULL pointer (also of $4$ bytes). Suppose a file of $1 \text{ M}$ bytes needs to be stored in the disk. Assume, $1 \mathrm{~K}=2^{10}$ and $1 \mathrm{M}=2^{20}$. The amount of space in bytes that will be wasted due to internal fragmentation is __________. (Answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown:
Disk block size $=64K=2^{16}$ bytes. In linked allocation, every block (including the last) reserves $4$ bytes for its "next" pointer field, leaving usable data capacity per block $=65536-4=65532$ bytes.

File size $=1M=2^{20}=1{,}048{,}576$ bytes. Number of blocks needed $=\lceil1{,}048{,}576/65532\rceil$: since $65532\times16=1{,}048{,}512$ (short of the file size by $64$ bytes), a $17$th block is required, giving $17$ blocks total.

Total disk space allocated $=17\times65536=1{,}114{,}112$ bytes. Space genuinely "useful" (actual file data plus the $4$-byte pointer overhead in each of the $17$ blocks) $=1{,}048{,}576+17\times4=1{,}048{,}576+68=1{,}048{,}644$ bytes.

Internal fragmentation (wasted space) $=1{,}114{,}112-1{,}048{,}644=65{,}468$ bytes.

go:460038.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 42
go:460038.question:
Refer to the given $3$-address code sequence. This code sequence is split into basic blocks. The number of basic blocks is ________. (Answer in integer)

1001: i = 1
1002: j = 1
1003: t1 = 10*i
1004: t2 = t1+j
1005: t3 = 8*t2
1006: t4 = t3-88
1007: a[t4] = 0.0
1008: j = j+1
1009: if j <= 10 goto 1003
1010: i = i+1
1011: if i <= 10 goto 1002
1012: i = 1
1013: t5 = i-1
1014: t6 = 88*t5
1015: a[t6] = 1.0
1016: i = i+1
1017: if i <= 10 goto 1013

detailed_solution.markdown: A new basic block begins at every leader statement: the very first statement, any statement that is the target of a jump/goto, and any statement immediately following a conditional or unconditional jump. Scanning the code for leaders: $1001$ (first statement); $1003$ (target of the $\text{goto }1003$ at $1009$); $1010$ (follows the conditional jump at $1009$); $1002$ (target of $\text{goto }1002$ at $1011$); $1012$ (follows the conditional jump at $1011$); $1013$ (target of $\text{goto }1013$ at $1017$). That's $6$ leaders, giving $6$ basic blocks: $\{1001\},\{1002\},\{1003\text{-}1009\},\{1010\text{-}1011\},\{1012\},\{1013\text{-}1017\}$.

go:460037.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 43
go:460037.question: A computer has a memory hierarchy consisting of two-level cache $\text{(L1}$ and $\text{L2)}$ and a main memory. If the processor needs to access data from memory, it first looks into $\text{L1}$ cache. If the data is not found in $\text{L1}$ cache, it goes to $\text{L2}$ cache. If it fails to get the data from $\text{L2}$ cache, it goes to main memory, where the data is definitely available. Hit rates and access times of various memory units are shown in the figure. The average memory access time in nanoseconds $(n s)$ is ________. (rounded off to two decimal places)

detailed_solution.markdown: This system uses hierarchical (serial) cache access: to reach L2, the processor must have already tried and missed in L1; to reach main memory, it must have already tried and missed in both L1 and L2. This means the given access-time figures for L2 and main memory already include the time already spent checking the earlier levels: L1 access time $T_1=10$ ns, L2 access time (which already includes the L1 miss penalty) $T_2=20$ ns, and main memory access time (already including both L1 and L2 miss penalties) $T_3=200$ ns. Hit rates: $H_1=0.95$ (L1), $H_2=0.85$ (L2). The average memory access time is a weighted sum over the three possible outcomes — hit in L1, miss-L1-then-hit-L2, or miss-both-then-go-to-memory: $\text{AMAT}=H_1T_1+(1-H_1)H_2T_2+(1-H_1)(1-H_2)T_3$ $=0.95(10)+0.05(0.85)(20)+0.05(0.15)(200)$ $=9.5+0.85+1.5=11.85$ ns.

go:460036.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 44
go:460036.question:
In optimal page replacement algorithm, information about all future page references is available to the operating system (OS). A modification of the optimal page replacement algorithm is as follows:

The OS correctly predicts only up to next $4$ page references (including the current page) at the time of allocating a frame to a page.

A process accesses the pages in the following order of page numbers:
$$1,3,2,4,2,3,1,2,4,3,1,4$$
If the system has three memory frames that are initially empty, the number of page faults that will occur during execution of the process is __________. (Answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown:
With the OS able to correctly predict only the next $4$ references (including the current one) at the moment a frame is allocated, simulate the reference string $1,3,2,4,2,3,1,2,4,3,1,4$ with $3$ initially-empty frames:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c}\text{Ref}&\text{Frames after}&\text{Fault?}\\\hline1&\{1\}&\text{Fault}\\3&\{1,3\}&\text{Fault}\\2&\{1,3,2\}&\text{Fault}\\4&\{4,3,2\}\ (\text{evict }1\text{, unused within next window }2,3,1)&\text{Fault}\\2&\{4,3,2\}&\text{Hit}\\3&\{4,3,2\}&\text{Hit}\\1&\{4,2,1\}\ (\text{evict }3\text{, farthest-future within window }2,4,3)&\text{Fault}\\2&\{4,2,1\}&\text{Hit}\\4&\{4,2,1\}&\text{Hit}\\3&\{4,1,3\}\ (\text{evict }2\text{, no longer used in remaining string})&\text{Fault}\\1&\{4,1,3\}&\text{Hit}\\4&\{4,1,3\}&\text{Hit}\end{array}$$

Total page faults $=6$ (at references $1,3,2,4,1,3$ in the sequence, marked "Fault" above).

    )
