go:460034.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 46
go:460034.question: Suppose a $5$-bit message is transmitted from a source to a destination through a noisy channel. The probability that a bit of the message gets flipped during transmission is $0.01$. Flipping of each bit is independent of one another. The probability that the message is delivered error-free to the destination is ___________ (rounded off to three decimal places)

detailed_solution.markdown: Each of the $5$ bits is flipped independently with probability $0.01$, so each bit survives correctly with probability $0.99$. The whole message arrives error-free only if every bit survives: $P(\text{error-free})=(0.99)^5\approx0.951$

go:460033.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 47
go:460033.question: Suppose a message of size $15000$ bytes is transmitted from a source to a destination using IPv4 protocol via two routers as shown in the figure. Each router has a defined maximum transmission unit (MTU) as shown in the figure, including IP header. The number of fragments that will be delivered to the destination is _________. (Answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown: Assume the standard $20$-byte IPv4 header (no options), so the original datagram is $15000+20=15020$ bytes. At Router-1 (MTU $5000$): max data per fragment $=5000-20=4980$ bytes, but fragment data must be a multiple of $8$ bytes, so usable data per (non-last) fragment $=\lfloor4980/8\rfloor\times8=4976$ bytes. $15000$ bytes of data $\div4976\approx3.01$: so $3$ full fragments of $4976$ bytes ($14928$ bytes) plus a final fragment of $15000-14928=72$ bytes. Total after Router-1: 4 fragments. At Router-2 (MTU $3000$): each fragment bigger than $3000$ bytes must be split again; the small $72$-byte-data fragment (total size $92$ bytes) passes straight through unchanged. Max data per new sub-fragment $=3000-20=2980$, rounded down to a multiple of $8$: $\lfloor2980/8\rfloor\times8=2976$ bytes. Each of the $3$ big fragments (data $=4976$ bytes) splits into: one sub-fragment of $2976$ bytes, plus a final sub-fragment of $4976-2976=2000$ bytes — $2$ sub-fragments each, so $3\times2=6$ sub-fragments total. Total fragments reaching the destination $=6$ (from the split large fragments) $+1$ (the small fragment that passed through) $=7$.

go:460032.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 48
go:460032.question:
Consider a probability distribution given by the density function $P(x)$.
$$P(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}
C x^{2}, & \text { for } 1 \leq x \leq 4 \\
0, & \text { for } x<1 \text { or } x>4
\end{aligned}\right.$$
The probability that $x$ lies between $2$ and $3$, i.e., $P(2 \leq x \leq 3)$ is _________. (rounded off to three decimal places)

detailed_solution.markdown:
First find $C$ using the normalization condition $\int_1^4Cx^2\,dx=1$:

$C\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_1^4=C\cdot\dfrac{64-1}{3}=21C=1\ \Rightarrow\ C=\dfrac1{21}$

$$P(2\le x\le3)=\displaystyle\int_2^3\dfrac{x^2}{21}\,dx=\dfrac1{21}\left[\dfrac{x^3}3\right]_2^3=\dfrac1{21}\cdot\dfrac{27-8}3=\dfrac1{21}\cdot\dfrac{19}3=\dfrac{19}{63}\approx0.302$$

go:460031.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 49
go:460031.question:
Consider a finite state machine (FSM) with one input $X$ and one output $f$, represented by the given state transition table. The minimum number of states required to realize this FSM is _______. (Answer in integer).                                                                                                           

$$\overset{\Large{\text{Present state        Next state             Output f}}}{\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline
\text{ $\qquad\qquad\qquad$} & \text{X=0} &  \text{X=1} & \text{X=0} &  \text{X=1}  \\ 
\hline
\text{A} & \text{F} & \text{B} & \text{0} & \text{0}  \\  \hline
\text{B} & \text{D} & \text{C} & \text{0} & \text{0}  \\  \hline
\text{C} & \text{F} & \text{E} & \text{0} & \text{0}  \\  \hline
\text{D} & \text{G} & \text{A} & \text{1} & \text{0}  \\  \hline \text{E} & \text{D} & \text{C} & \text{0} & \text{0}  \\  \hline \text{F} & \text{F} & \text{B} & \text{1} & \text{1}  \\  \hline \text{G} & \text{G} & \text{H} & \text{0} & \text{1}  \\  \hline \text{H} & \text{G} & \text{A} & \text{1} & \text{0}  \\  \hline \end{array}}$$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Group states by their immediate output behavior first: states with outputs $(f_0,f_1)=(0,0)$ are $\{A,B,C,E\}$; $(1,0)$ are $\{D,H\}$; $(1,1)$ is $\{F\}$; $(0,1)$ is $\{G\}$ — four initial groups.

Refine $\{A,B,C,E\}$ by checking which group each state's next-states fall into: $A$ and $C$ both go to (group-of-$F$, group-of-$\{A,B,C,E\}$) on $(X{=}0,X{=}1)$, while $B$ and $E$ both go to (group-of-$\{D,H\}$, group-of-$\{A,B,C,E\}$). So this group splits into $\{A,C\}$ and $\{B,E\}$.

Checking again with the new, finer partition $\{A,C\},\{B,E\},\{D,H\},\{F\},\{G\}$: every state's next-state signature now matches consistently within its own group (e.g. both $A$ and $C$ go to $F$ on $0$ and into $\{B,E\}$ on $1$; both $D$ and $H$ go to $G$ on $0$ and into $\{A,C\}$ on $1$) — so the partition is stable and no further splitting occurs.

Final equivalence classes: $\{A,C\},\{B,E\},\{D,H\},\{F\},\{G\}$ — $5$ classes.

go:460030.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 50
go:460030.question: Consider the given sequential circuit designed using D-Flip-flops. The circuit is initialized with some value (initial state). The number of distinct states the circuit will go through before returning back to the initial state is ___________. (Answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown: This circuit is a $4$-bit twisted-ring (Johnson) counter: the flip-flops are connected in a shift-register chain ($Q_0\to D_1,\ Q_1\to D_2,\ Q_2\to D_3$), with the feedback from the last stage back into $D_0$ being inverted. A Johnson counter built from $n$ flip-flops with inverted feedback is well known to cycle through $2n$ distinct states before returning to its starting state (e.g. starting from $0000$: $0000\to1000\to1100\to1110\to1111\to0111\to0011\to0001\to0000$). For $n=4$ flip-flops, that's $2\times4=8$ states in the full cycle — i.e. $7$ other distinct states are visited before the circuit returns to repeat its initial state (with the full period being $8$ steps, depending on whether the initial state itself is counted in the tally).

go:460029.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 51
go:460029.question:
#include <stdio.h>
int foo(int S,int size) {
    if(size == 0) return 0;
    if(size == 1) return 1;
    if(S[0] != S[1]) return 1+foo(S+1,size-1);
    return foo(S+1,size-1);
}
int main() {
    int A={0,1,2,2,2,0,0,1,1};
    printf("%d",foo(A,9));
    return 0;
}

The value printed by the given $C$ program is ___________. (Answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown:
Trace the recursion on $A=[0,1,2,2,2,0,0,1,1]$ (comparing each element to its immediate neighbor, adding $1$ whenever they differ):

$$\begin{array}{l}foo([0,1,\ldots])=1+foo([1,2,\ldots])\quad(0\ne1)\\foo([1,2,\ldots])=1+foo([2,2,\ldots])\quad(1\ne2)\\foo([2,2,2,0,\ldots])=foo([2,2,0,\ldots])\quad(2=2)\\foo([2,2,0,\ldots])=foo([2,0,0,\ldots])\quad(2=2)\\foo([2,0,0,1,1])=1+foo([0,0,1,1])\quad(2\ne0)\\foo([0,0,1,1])=foo([0,1,1])\quad(0=0)\\foo([0,1,1])=1+foo([1,1])\quad(0\ne1)\\foo([1,1])=foo([1])\quad(1=1)\\foo([1])=1\quad(\text{base case, size}=1)\end{array}$$

Unwinding: $foo([1,1])=1$, $foo([0,1,1])=1+1=2$, $foo([0,0,1,1])=2$, $foo([2,0,0,1,1])=1+2=3$, $foo([2,2,0,\ldots])=3$, $foo([2,2,2,\ldots])=3$, $foo([1,2,\ldots])=1+3=4$, $foo([0,1,\ldots])=1+4=5$.

go:460028.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 52
go:460028.question:
Let $\mathrm{LIST}$ be a datatype for an implementation of linked list defined as follows:

typedef struct list {
int data;
struct list *next;
} LIST;

Suppose a program has created two linked lists, $L1$ and $L2$, whose contents are given in the figure below (code for creating $L1$ and $L2$ is not provided here). $L1$ contains $9$ nodes, and $L2$ contains $7$ nodes.

Consider the following C program segment that modifies the list $L1$. The number of nodes that will be there in $L1$ after the execution of the code segment is __________. (Answer in integer)

int find (int query, LIST *list) {
while (list != NULL) {
if(list->data == query) return 1 ;
list = list->next;
}
return 0 ;
}
int main() {
... ... ...
ptr1=L1; ptr2=L2;
while (ptr1->next != NULL){
query = ptr1->next->data;
if (find (query, L2))
ptr1->next = ptr1->next->next;
else ptr1 = ptr1->next;
}
... .... ...
return 0;
}

detailed_solution.markdown: From the given lists, $L1: 1,7,12,3,9,5,11,15,8$ and $L2:1,11,6,9,15,12,4$ (so $L2=\{1,11,6,9,15,12,4\}$ as a lookup set). The code walks $ptr1$ through $L1$, and for each node, looks at the next node's value: if that value is found anywhere in $L2$, the next node is unlinked (removed) and $ptr1$ stays put (to re-check the new next node); otherwise $ptr1$ simply advances. Tracing through: starting value $7$ (not in L2) → advance. Next value $12$ (in L2) → delete $12$. Next value $3$ (not in L2) → advance. Next value $9$ (in L2) → delete $9$. Next value $5$ (not in L2) → advance. Next value $11$ (in L2) → delete $11$. Next value $15$ (in L2) → delete $15$. Next value $8$ (not in L2) → advance; now at the last node, loop ends. Nodes removed: $12,9,11,15$ ($4$ nodes), leaving $9-4=5$ nodes: $1,7,3,5,8$.

go:460027.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 53
go:460027.question:
Consider the following C program:

#include <stdio.h>
int gate (int n) {
int d, t, newnum, turn;
newnum = turn = 0; t=1;
while (n>=t) t *= 10;
t /=10;
while (t>0) {
d = n/t;
n = n%t;
t /= 10;
if (turn) newnum = 10*newnum + d;
turn = (turn + 1) % 2;
}
return newnum;
}
int main  {
printf ("%d", gate(14362));
return 0;
}

The value printed by the given $C$ program is ________. (Answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown: $\text{gate(14362)}$ first works out that $14362$ has $5$ digits (via the $t$-scaling loop), then peels off digits from most significant to least significant, keeping every other digit starting from the 2nd digit (since $turn$ starts at $0$ — skip, then keep, skip, keep, ...). Digits of $14362$ in order: $1,4,3,6,2$. $turn=0$: digit $1$ — skipped. $turn=1$: digit $4$ — kept, $newnum=4$. $turn=0$: digit $3$ — skipped. $turn=1$: digit $6$ — kept, $newnum=4\times10+6=46$. $turn=0$: digit $2$ — skipped. Final $newnum=46$.

go:460026.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 54
go:460026.question: The maximum value of $\text{x}$ such that the edge between the nodes $\text{B}$ and $\text{C}$ is included in every minimum spanning tree of the given graph is _________. (answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown: From the given graph (vertices A, B, C, D with edges $AB{=}7,\ AD{=}6,\ CD{=}8,\ AC{=}1,\ BD{=}3$, and $BC{=}x$), we want the largest $x$ for which edge $BC$ is forced into every MST. Checking systematically for increasing $x$ (e.g. by comparing the total weight of all spanning trees that include $BC$ versus all spanning trees that exclude it): for $x\le5$, every minimum spanning tree happens to include edge $BC$ (any spanning tree avoiding it ends up strictly heavier, since the cheapest way to connect $B$ and $C$'s side of the graph without directly using $BC$ costs strictly more than $5$ extra). But once $x=6$, an alternative spanning tree that avoids edge $BC$ entirely becomes just as cheap (tied for minimum), so $BC$ is no longer forced into every MST. So the maximum value of $x$ that still guarantees $BC$ is in every MST is the last value before this tie appears.

go:460025.title: GATE CSE 2025 | Set 1 | Question: 55
go:460025.question:
In a double hashing scheme, $h_{1}(k)=k \bmod 11$ and $h_{2}(k)=1+(k \bmod 7)$ are the auxiliary hash functions. The size $m$ of the hash table is $11$. The hash function for the $i$-th probe in the open address table is $\left[h_{1}(k)+i h_{2}(k)\right] \bmod m$. The following keys are inserted in the given order: $63,50,25,79,67,24$.

The slot at which key $24$ gets stored is ___________ . (Answer in integer)

detailed_solution.markdown:
Double hashing: $h_1(k)=k\bmod11$, $h_2(k)=1+(k\bmod7)$, probe $i$: $[h_1(k)+ih_2(k)]\bmod11$, table size $11$.

Insert in order, computing initial slot (and probing forward on collision):

$63$: $h_1=8$ → slot $8$ (empty).

$50$: $h_1=6$ → slot $6$ (empty).

$25$: $h_1=3$ → slot $3$ (empty).

$79$: $h_1=2$ → slot $2$ (empty).

$67$: $h_1=1$ → slot $1$ (empty).

$24$: $h_1=2$ (taken by $79$), $h_2=1+(24\bmod7)=1+3=4$. Probe $i=1$: $(2+4)\bmod11=6$ (taken by $50$). Probe $i=2$: $(2+8)\bmod11=10$ (empty) → placed at slot $10$.
